catalog_quote: [p.76] Every stress group contains only one word but may also contain one or more phonologically dependent clitics which may form immediate constituents with that word or with the phrase as a whole. The morphological barrier between word and clitic is symbolized by a hyphen. The placement of stress is predictable on the grammatical level. Since it is not predictable on a phonological level we are treating it as a phoneme and symbolizing it with a ´. Within the word, stress occurs on the final long vowel or on the final short vowel if no long vowels are present. The prosodic features of emphatic stress and possible intonational pitch within the phrase have not yet been satisfactorily analyzed though some features have been noted. sweep_summary: the list of works with stress in the title for agua1252 holds a single title, McArthur & McArthur 1956 (IJAL 22(1):72-76), which is already the catalog's deciding source. The U Chicago DOI landing page is paywalled (not reachable by automated download to the fetcher), but an unrestricted archive.org microfilm scan of the whole issue is held by the project (downloaded 2026-09-12 into the the weight-sensitive languages our files; still downloadable, HEAD 200, 22.35 MB) and I re-read journal p.76 from the page image: 'Within the word, stress occurs on the final long vowel or on the final short vowel if no long vowels are present', clitics outside the word domain, stronger phrase stress usually on the last word. This confirms the catalog's 'weight' classification verbatim; nothing supersedes it. Copies of the p.76 page image, the p.72-76 and p.76 text extracts and the archive.org metadata were placed in and logged in there. As on-disk context (not in the title list) I also read ALMG 2013 Gramática Normativa Awakateka section 2.3.3 (p.108-109): stress 'fijo.. la última' syllable for polysyllables, with a note that some words show socially conditioned penult/final free variation; vowel length is not written, so it neither tests nor contradicts the long-vowel condition; it refines (default-final agrees; adds a free-variation caveat) rather than contradicts. Larsen 1983 (held by the project, our earlier reading) p.141 notes one marked exception (che7-ch 'they said' with stress on the absolutive prefix vowel). No new open sources were found;org metadata. Nothing remains to acquire for this language (priority none).

new_statements.reading: Quantity-sensitive, unbounded: within the grammatical word (clitics excluded) primary stress is on the rightmost long-vowel syllable; with no long vowel it defaults to the final syllable. Heavy = long vowel only (five long-vowel phonemes, p.72); closed syllables and V+glottal-stop are not said to attract stress. This is exactly the catalog's 'weight' coding (rightmost heavy else final).

sources.locator: p.76, section 3 'Stress', left column, with fn. 8; vowel inventory (five short, five long vowels) p.72 section 1
sources.note: Word stress (domain = grammatical word, clitics excluded) falls on the rightmost long vowel; if the word has no long vowel, on the final syllable. Stated flatly, no exceptions listed. A stronger phrase stress usually sits on the stressed syllable of the last word of the phrase; emphatic stress and intonation not analysed. Fn. 8: stress could be treated as non-phonemic but grammatically conditioned if word/clitic grouping is admitted as a conditioning basis. Data are from the Chalchitán dialect, 1953-54 fieldwork.

sources.locator: section 2.3.3 'Acento', printed pp.108-109 (PDF pp.107-108; lines 7125-7185); 'Vocales Prolongadas' section ( lines 6631-6650)
sources.note: Normative grammar: stress is fixed on the final syllable of polysyllables (examples of 2-, 3- and 4+-syllable words all final-stressed, p.109); stress is not semantically distinctive; in some words penult/final stress alternates in socially conditioned free variation (examples txikun 'bean', saja'ch 'to play', meb'a' 'poor', p.109). The orthography does not write vowel length, so the long-vowel condition of McArthur & McArthur is not addressed.
